subtopic: States of Matter, Phase Changes and Diffusion
stem: Which of the following is a characteristic property of the gaseous state of matter?
optB: Definite volume but no definite shape
optC: Neither definite shape nor definite volume
solution: A gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume; it fills the entire container it occupies and is highly compressible. A solid has both definite shape and volume; a liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape. Matches option C.

subtopic: States of Matter, Phase Changes and Diffusion
stem: The process by which a solid changes directly into vapour without passing through the liquid state is called
solution: The direct solid-to-vapour transition (e.g. of camphor, naphthalene, dry ice) is sublimation. Vaporisation is liquid to vapour, condensation is vapour to liquid, and effusion is the escape of gas through a tiny hole. Matches option B.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: Which of the following is an intensive property of matter?
solution: An intensive property does not depend on the amount of substance. Density (mass per unit volume) is the same for any sample of a given material, so it is intensive. Mass, volume and length all scale with the amount of matter, so they are extensive. Matches option C.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: The number of significant figures in the measurement \(0.00420\) g is
solution: Leading zeros are not significant, so the zeros before 4 do not count. The significant digits are 4, 2 and the trailing 0 (a trailing zero after the decimal point is significant), giving three significant figures. Matches option B.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: SI unit of amount of substance is
solution: The SI base unit for the amount of substance is the mole. Kilogram is the unit of mass, candela of luminous intensity, and kelvin of thermodynamic temperature. Matches option B.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: A student measures the volume of a liquid three times and obtains values very close to the true value each time. The measurement is best described as having high
solution: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings to one another. Values that are very close to the true value on every trial are both near the truth (accurate) and consistent with each other (precise). Matches option C.

subtopic: Atomic Models: Dalton, Rutherford, Bohr
stem: According to Dalton's atomic theory, atoms of the same element are
optB: Different in mass but identical in properties
solution: Dalton postulated that all atoms of a given element are identical in mass and in their chemical properties. (This postulate was later modified by the discovery of isotopes.) Matches option A.

subtopic: Atomic Models: Dalton, Rutherford, Bohr
stem: Which postulate of Dalton's atomic theory was later found to be incorrect after the discovery of isotopes?
optA: Atoms combine in simple whole number ratios
optB: Atoms of the same element are identical in mass
optC: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
solution: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different masses (different numbers of neutrons), which contradicts Dalton's postulate that all atoms of an element are identical in mass. Matches option B.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: Dalton's atomic theory explains which of the following laws?
optA: Law of conservation of mass only
optC: Both law of conservation of mass and law of definite proportions
solution: Because atoms are merely rearranged (neither created nor destroyed) and combine in fixed ratios, Dalton's theory accounts for both the law of conservation of mass and the law of definite proportions (and multiple proportions). Avogadro's law follows from Avogadro's hypothesis, not Dalton's theory. Matches option C.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: 12 g of carbon combines with 32 g of oxygen to form carbon dioxide. This is an illustration of the law of
solution: Carbon and oxygen always combine in the fixed mass ratio \(12:32 = 3:8\) to form carbon dioxide, regardless of the source. A fixed combining ratio of elements in a compound is the law of definite (constant) proportions. Matches option B.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: Carbon combines with oxygen to form CO and \(\text{CO}_2\), in which the masses of oxygen combining with a fixed mass of carbon are in a simple whole number ratio. This illustrates the law of
solution: For a fixed 12 g of carbon, CO has 16 g of oxygen and \(\text{CO}_2\) has 32 g, a ratio of \(16:32 = 1:2\), a simple whole number ratio. When two elements form more than one compound and the masses of one combining with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple ratio, it is the law of multiple proportions. Matches option B.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: The law of conservation of mass states that
optA: Mass can be created but not destroyed
optB: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
optC: Mass is always converted into energy
optD: Total mass of reactants is always greater than that of products
solution: The law of conservation of mass states that in a chemical reaction matter can neither be created nor destroyed; the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. Matches option B.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: Two elements A and B combine separately with a fixed mass of element C. If A and B also combine with each other, the ratio of their masses is related to the masses in which they combine with C. This is a statement of the law of
solution: The law of reciprocal proportions states that the ratio of masses of two elements A and B that combine with a fixed mass of a third element C is the same as (or a simple multiple of) the ratio in which A and B combine directly with each other. Matches option A.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes is best explained on the basis of
solution: Avogadro's hypothesis, that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, explains why gases react in simple whole number volume ratios (Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes). Dalton's atomic theory could not account for combining volumes. Matches option B.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: 6 g of magnesium burns in oxygen to form 10 g of magnesium oxide. The mass of oxygen consumed is
solution: By the law of conservation of mass, mass of oxygen \(=\) mass of product \(-\) mass of magnesium \(= 10 - 6 = 4\) g. Matches option A.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: The empirical formula of a compound represents
optA: The exact number of atoms of each element in a molecule
optB: The simplest whole number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound
optC: The molecular mass of the compound
solution: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole number ratio of the atoms of each element present in a compound. The exact number of atoms per molecule is the molecular formula. Matches option B.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: A compound has the empirical formula \(\text{CH}_2\text{O}\) and a molecular mass of 180 g/mol. Its molecular formula is
solution: Empirical formula mass of \(\text{CH}_2\text{O} = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30\) g/mol. Then \(n = 180/30 = 6\), so the molecular formula is \((\text{CH}_2\text{O})_6 = \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\). Matches option C.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: An organic compound contains 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its empirical formula is
solution: Relative moles: C \(= 40/12 = 3.33\), H \(= 6.7/1 = 6.7\), O \(= 53.3/16 = 3.33\). Dividing by the smallest (3.33) gives \(1:2:1\), so the empirical formula is \(\text{CH}_2\text{O}\). Matches option A.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: The relationship between molecular formula and empirical formula is given by
optA: Molecular formula = Empirical formula \(\times\) n, where n is a whole number
optD: Molecular formula is always equal to the empirical formula
solution: The molecular formula is a whole number multiple of the empirical formula: molecular formula \(=\) (empirical formula) \(\times n\), where \(n =\) molecular mass / empirical formula mass. Matches option A.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: A hydrocarbon has an empirical formula of \(\text{CH}_2\) and a vapour density of 21. Its molecular formula is
solution: Molar mass \(= 2 \times\) vapour density \(= 2 \times 21 = 42\) g/mol. Empirical formula mass of \(\text{CH}_2 = 14\), so \(n = 42/14 = 3\), giving \((\text{CH}_2)_3 = \text{C}_3\text{H}_6\). Matches option B.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: In the reaction \(\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3\), how many moles of \(\text{NH}_3\) are produced from 2 moles of \(\text{N}_2\), assuming excess \(\text{H}_2\) is available?
solution: The equation shows 1 mol \(\text{N}_2\) gives 2 mol \(\text{NH}_3\). With excess hydrogen, 2 mol \(\text{N}_2\) gives \(2 \times 2 = 4\) mol \(\text{NH}_3\). Matches option C.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: The number of moles of oxygen molecules required to completely burn 2 moles of methane \((\text{CH}_4 + 2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O})\) is
solution: The equation requires 2 mol \(\text{O}_2\) per 1 mol \(\text{CH}_4\). For 2 mol methane, oxygen needed \(= 2 \times 2 = 4\) mol. Matches option C.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: Calculate the mass of \(\text{CO}_2\) produced when 4.4 g of propane \((\text{C}_3\text{H}_8)\) undergoes complete combustion. (Molar mass: \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 = 44\) g/mol, \(\text{CO}_2 = 44\) g/mol)
solution: Moles of propane \(= 4.4/44 = 0.1\) mol. Combustion: \(\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}\), so each mole of propane gives 3 mol \(\text{CO}_2\). Moles of \(\text{CO}_2 = 0.1 \times 3 = 0.3\); mass \(= 0.3 \times 44 = 13.2\) g. Matches option C.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: How many grams of water are produced when 8 g of hydrogen gas reacts completely with excess oxygen? \((2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O})\)
solution: Moles of \(\text{H}_2 = 8/2 = 4\) mol. The equation gives 2 mol \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) per 2 mol \(\text{H}_2\), so moles of water \(= 4\); mass \(= 4 \times 18 = 72\) g. Matches option C.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: The percentage composition of nitrogen in ammonia \((\text{NH}_3\), molar mass 17 g/mol) is approximately
solution: Mass of nitrogen in one mole of \(\text{NH}_3\) is 14 g out of 17 g. Percentage \(= (14/17) \times 100 \approx 82.4\%\). Matches option D.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: The percentage of oxygen by mass in water \((\text{H}_2\text{O})\) is closest to
solution: Molar mass of water \(= 18\) g/mol, of which oxygen is 16 g. Percentage of oxygen \(= (16/18) \times 100 \approx 88.9\%\), closest to 89%. Matches option D.

subtopic: Mole Concept, Avogadro's Law and Molar Calculations
stem: A compound is found to contain 40% sulfur and 60% oxygen by mass. If the molar mass of the compound is 80 g/mol, its molecular formula is
solution: Relative moles: S \(= 40/32 = 1.25\), O \(= 60/16 = 3.75\). Dividing by 1.25 gives \(1:3\), so the empirical formula is \(\text{SO}_3\) (empirical mass \(= 32 + 48 = 80\)). Since this equals the molar mass, the molecular formula is also \(\text{SO}_3\). Matches option B.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: In a reaction between 4 mol of \(\text{H}_2\) and 1 mol of \(\text{N}_2\) to form \(\text{NH}_3\) \((\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3)\), the limiting reagent is
solution: 1 mol \(\text{N}_2\) requires 3 mol \(\text{H}_2\). Only 3 of the 4 available moles of hydrogen are needed, so hydrogen is in excess and nitrogen is completely consumed first, making \(\text{N}_2\) the limiting reagent. Matches option B.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: The reagent that gets completely consumed first in a chemical reaction, thereby limiting the amount of product formed, is called the
solution: By definition, the reactant that is used up first and therefore determines (limits) how much product can form is the limiting reagent. Matches option B.

subtopic: Stoichiometry and Laws of Chemical Combination
stem: 5 moles of Al react with 6 moles of \(\text{Cl}_2\) as per the equation \(2\text{Al} + 3\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3\). The limiting reagent and the maximum moles of \(\text{AlCl}_3\) formed are
solution: The ratio needed is 2 Al : 3 \(\text{Cl}_2\). To react all 5 mol Al would need \(5 \times 3/2 = 7.5\) mol \(\text{Cl}_2\), but only 6 mol are available, so \(\text{Cl}_2\) is limiting. From 6 mol \(\text{Cl}_2\), \(\text{AlCl}_3 = 6 \times 2/3 = 4\) mol. Matches option B.
